name: Rhassoul clay

lead: Rhassoul (also ghassoul) is a smectite clay from Morocco's Middle Atlas, mixed with water and sometimes herbs to cleanse skin and hair. It is a traditional part of the Moroccan hammam, applied as a face mask or body poultice.
It is used for appearance as a cleansing mask that leaves skin and hair feeling clean and soft. Research is limited to mineral characterisation and a small case series on peristomal skin.

paras: The powdered clay is mixed with water into a paste and applied to the face, body or hair, and then rinsed. In hammam practice it is sometimes used with a glove or kessa exfoliating mitt. Users sometimes add herbs or other ingredients.

No safety studies on cosmetic use are cited here. Clays can be drying or irritating for some skin, and a mineral study found the clay can adsorb metal ions in lab conditions. A case series described its use on irritated skin around ostomies in Morocco.

angle.text: Users apply it as a mask or wash to cleanse skin and hair as part of a traditional beauty routine. Its mineral content gives it the ability to adsorb substances in lab tests.

lead: Rhassoul, also spelled ghassoul, is a smectite clay-based cosmetic made from mineral clay mined in the Middle Atlas of Morocco, mixed with water and sometimes herbs to cleanse the body.[1] The mineral is identified as stevensite, a magnesium silicate, and its formula, surface area of 134 m2/g and cation exchange capacity of 76.5 meq/100 g were described in a 2005 study.[2]

In appearance routines it is used as a cleansing facial mask and hair wash, and in hammams as a body poultice, sometimes with a kessa mitt. Moroccan women have used it for centuries, with use believed to date to the 8th century, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Wikipedia notes there is little formal research on how well it works.[1] The published literature includes the mineral characterisation study and a 2018 case series of three patients using rhassoul on skin damage around ostomies.[2][3]
infobox: Silica, magnesium, iron, potassium, sodium, lithium[1]

paras: The clay comes from deposits near the Moulouya valley, about 200 km from Fes, and contains silica, iron, magnesium, potassium, sodium and lithium.[1] A 2005 paper characterised the Moroccan stevensite called rhassoul chemically and physically.[2]
It is mainly used in hammams, applied as a face mask or body poultice, sometimes with a glove or kessa, resembling a Western mud wrap.[1]

A 2018 case series in the British Journal of Nursing reported three patients with peristomal skin damage in whom rhassoul was used to manage and protect skin; its protective properties are believed to include absorbing and neutralising damaging substances and acting as a barrier.[3] A laboratory study found the clay adsorbs metal ions such as Cd, Cu, Mn, Pb and Zn from aqueous solutions.[2]
